text.p: Business conditions and employment prospects of the manufacturing sector in Australia's most populous state, New South Wales (NSW), continued to deteriorate in the September quarter, a survey found.
The results prompted the survey's authors, the Australian Business Chamber (ABC) and the State Bank of NSW (SBNSW), to jointly call for a further cut in official interest rates.

"The survey indicates the cut in official interest rates at the beginning of August and the Federal budget have not adequately stimulated industry confidence or activity," ABC managing director Philip Holt said in a statement.

The Reserve Bank of Australia cut official interest rates on July 31 by 0.5 percentage points to 7.0 percent. It was the first change in monetary policy since December 1994, and the first rate cut in three years.
The survey found that firms expected to reduce their employment levels by nearly 5,100 jobs in the next year.
"Extrapolated nationally, the survey indicates the manufacturing sector in Australia could see jobs losses in excess of 15,000 over the coming year," the survey found.
Only 10 percent of firms raised employment in the September quarter, with 27 percent shedding jobs. Small and medium firms were most optimistic on the employment outlook.
"Production, sales and profitability have been negative for the seventh consecutive quarter, while selling prices have been negative for four successive quarters," Holt said.
In the September quarter, 25 percent of firms reported an increase in production, with 30 percent reporting a decline.
Increased sales were seen in 25 percent of companies, against a decline in 33 percent, and while 21 percent saw a lift in profitability, 36 percent it was down, the survey found.
Although December quarter expectations were positive in all three areas, the survey noted expectations traditionally exceeded outcomes.
The survey also found that only 14 percent of firms were able to lift selling prices, with 68 percent holding them steady and 128 percent reducing prices.
SBNSW chief economist Hans Kunnen said the survey pointed to lower inflation and higher unemployment.
Activity was being constrained by a lack of confidence, and a further cut in rates could provide the needed stimulus, he said.
"Manufacturers continue to see rising costs for labour and raw materials yet are unable to obtain higher selling prices," Kunnen said.
"Unless profitability improves, more labour shedding seems inevitable," he said.

The brightest aspect of the survey was exports, with the percentage of firms exporting expected to reach record levels. Of the firms surveyed, 59 percent expect to be exporting in the December quarter, against 57 percent in the third quarter.
While the continued growth in exports was encouraging, it would also be good to see more domestic activity, Kunnen said.
As well, import competition was not abating, with 19 percent seeing further increases in competition in the September quarter.

Wage pressures were persistent in the quarter, and throughout 1996 had exceeded respondents expectations. In the quarter, 28 percent of firms reported rising wage costs while a further 20 expected higher costs in the December quarter.
The survey covered 506 manufacturing companies in NSW. These cmpanies employ about 126,000 people or about 30 percent of the state's manufacturing employment, the survey said.
